rows.notes: Strong on the rubric's own axes: edge cases are specific and numerous (settlement overage, override-after-window, mid-cycle lowering, no-op resubmit, boundary rejection), non-functional bars are all time-boxed, and the out-of-scope section names two concrete exclusions (per-category limits, joint accounts) with no leftover placeholders or comments. Docked for a chained Given/When/Then ('hard-declined, and decline reason appears... within 2 minutes') that asserts two outcomes in one Then, and for a soft internal-consistency wrinkle: the settlement-overage edge case says a crossed threshold can trigger a 'decline-reason entry at settlement' immediately after stating the already-authorized transaction is never retroactively declined, which reads as in tension without being resolved. On the held-out side it is highly scopeable (an engineer could break this into tickets with no follow-up questions) but never marks which claims came from the brief versus the author's own call, never states a stop/kill condition, and never mentions the complaint volume or problem evidence that motivates the story at all, which the anti-form instruction specifically flags as a real gap, not a stylistic one. All five probes answered correctly and precisely from the document alone.

Weaker on the rubric's structural axes than Artifact A: it has no dedicated Edge cases or Non-functional sections (that content is folded into numbered ACs), AC1 and AC5 each bundle more than one assertion into a single Given/When/Then, and AC2 is a meta-commentary item about UI-copy confidence rather than a testable criterion, which muddies the checklist. It is explicit and specific about scope (per-category limits excluded by name, including from UI as a 'coming soon' placeholder) and keeps every criterion tied to the story's actual behavior rather than generic bars. Where it pulls ahead is the held-out, decision-usefulness side: it states the motivating evidence (340 Q2 tickets) and ties the highest-risk criterion (AC5, the estimated-authorization edge case) directly back to that complaint pattern, and it explicitly marks which facts are given requirements versus which are open calls still needing a decision (AC5's exact rule, AC7's window start point) rather than presenting guesses as settled fact. That honesty cuts both ways: the single most load-bearing criterion for the story's stated purpose is left formally unresolved, which is a real gap against an ask that wanted this 'locked down' before sprint planning. All five probes still answered correctly, including the estimated-authorization question, though the document itself flags that answer as provisional pending a product call.

Every criterion, scenario, and non-functional item is a content-free placeholder ('will meet the needs of its intended users,' 'operate as intended across the applicable scenarios'); nothing is observable, measurable, or specific to this story, and the out-of-scope section names no actual exclusion. None of the five retrieval probes can be answered from this document: no limit bounds, no estimated-authorization handling, no override window or decline-visibility timing, no statement on per-category scope, no reset-date behavior. The internal-consistency held-out criterion gets a marginally non-zero score only because there is no concrete claim to contradict another concrete claim, not because the document demonstrates any real coherence. This reads as a generic shell with the story's nouns never substituted in.

Strong on observable/measurable content tied directly to the 340-ticket complaint (AC4) and on the hardest edge case (AC5, estimated/pending authorizations), stated in unambiguous terms as the scenario asks. Explicitly distinguishes what was given (bounds/increment: 'stated directly as a product requirement') from what still needs a decision (UI copy, AC5's exact implementation call, AC7's 5-minute start point) -- this is the only artifact that marks provenance this clearly, which is exactly the decision-vs-told held-out criterion. No distractor facts appear. Weaknesses: no separate Non-functional-criteria or formal Scenarios section, so the few measurable timing bars (2-minute decline-reason visibility, 5-minute override) sit inside numbered ACs rather than a distinct NFC block; only one edge case (AC5) is named with the depth the rubric wants, versus several in Artifact C. No stop/kill condition anywhere. All 5 probes answerable directly and correctly.

Entirely vacuous. Every checklist item, scenario, and non-functional entry is generic boilerplate ('will meet the needs of its intended users in a manner consistent with expectations') that would read identically if pasted onto any other story in the backlog -- the exact anti-pattern the no-dod-duplication criterion targets. No dollar figures, no timing, no named failure conditions, no real scope exclusions: the Given/When/Then scenarios have the right skeleton (one When, one Then) but name no actual behavior, so I scored that cell low rather than crediting empty structure. None of the 5 retrieval probes are answerable from this document; a reader cannot size work, test anything, or know what 'done' means from it alone. Internal-consistency and provenance-marking scored slightly above floor only because there is no concrete claim to contradict or attribute -- that is a vacuous pass, not a real one.

The most structurally complete on the rubric's own terms: a genuine Edge-cases section naming five distinct failure/boundary conditions (settlement overage, late override, mid-cycle lowering, no-op same-value change, out-of-range entry) each with a stated observable outcome, a real Non-functional-criteria section with numeric bars (2-minute, 5-minute), and four single-behavior Given/When/Then scenarios. This is genuine added substance, not just reformatting of the same facts -- it covers boundary behaviors (lowering limit mid-cycle, no-op edit) neither other artifact names. However, per the anti-form/distractor instruction I am penalizing it for pulling in distractor material not asked for: the Out-of-scope section adds 'Does not cover joint-account limit behavior,' which derives from the Legal distractor fact (joint-account question), and an assumption about 'the limits service' receiving data from card networks that echoes the microservices-ownership distractor -- both are scope creep the brief explicitly warned against ('do not let it balloon'). It also does not mark which claims were given to the author versus decided by the author the way Artifact A does (only one hedge, 'Assumes...'), so it scores lower than A on decision-vs-told. No stop/kill signal. All 5 probes answerable and correct.

Generic filler throughout. The document has no story text, no limit bounds, no reset rule, no holds edge case, no override or decline-reason timings, and no named exclusion. Every criterion is an unfalsifiable adjective ('as intended', 'appropriate', 'consistent with expectations'), and the scenarios are content-free. Rubric scores are all 1. On the held-out criteria, internal-consistency gets a 2 only because the document says too little to contradict itself. Every other held-out criterion scores 1.

This is the most complete and most testable of the three, and it answers all five probes. It gives the $100-$10,000 range in $50 steps and says the limit resets on the cardholder's own statement date. It says estimated holds are not retroactively declined and that the overage counts at settlement. It gives the 5-minute override and the 2-minute decline reason, and it excludes per-category limits as unscoped and unfunded. The edge cases are specific and testable: the expired override window, lowering the limit mid-cycle below spend already made, a no-op change, and out-of-range values. Its main defect sits in the core rule. The rule says 'once cumulative spend reaches or exceeds the limit, the NEXT authorization is declined', which lets one transaction carry spend well past the cap. That is the exact complaint the ask wanted made airtight, so it is not a nitpick. Scenario 2 chains two assertions in its Then (decline AND reason in history). The 2-minute notification bar in the non-functional criteria is invented, and it is not marked as the author's choice. Several other author choices (no-op handling, mid-cycle lowering) read the same as mandates, so decision-vs-told scores 2. The edge case says crossing 100% at settlement 'triggers the decline-reason entry' even though nothing was declined, which is a mild internal tension. It partly leaks two distractors: joint-account behaviour appears as an exclusion, and the 'limits service' appears in the assumptions. No stop or kill condition appears anywhere. Scores: observable 4, unhappy paths 4, no DoD duplication 4, measurable NFR 4, single-behaviour scenarios 3, scope 4. Held-out: scopeable 4, stop/kill 1, consistency 3, decided-vs-told 2.

This one also answers all five probes, and it states the core decline rule correctly: a transaction that WOULD push spend past the limit is declined. It also asks QA to test the exact-remaining-balance boundary. It is the best of the three at telling decided from told. It marks confidence and provenance ('stated directly as a product requirement'), it says the placeholder copy is for design to decide, and it lists unknowns explicitly, including when the override window starts. It carries no distractors. Its structural weaknesses are real. AC2 is a confidence note numbered as an acceptance criterion, and AC9 is an out-of-scope statement numbered the same way. It has no non-functional section and no measurable non-functional bar (the 90% notification has no timing). It has no discrete Given/When/Then scenarios, and AC1 bundles several behaviours. It names fewer unhappy paths than B: it misses lowering the limit mid-cycle and repeated or invalid changes. It is internally inconsistent: AC5 states a specific treatment for holds, then the Unknowns section says that rule has not been decided. It leaks process language ('not in the What you know input'), and it adds unmarked choices of its own ('no default limit', 'fires once per cycle'). No stop or kill condition appears. Scores: observable 3, unhappy paths 3, no DoD duplication 4, measurable NFR 2, single-behaviour scenarios 2, scope 4. Held-out: scopeable 3, stop/kill 1, consistency 2, decided-vs-told 4.

Rubric cells: observable-verifiable 4 (concrete, pass/fail phrasing throughout; 'takes effect immediately' is the one soft spot); unhappy-paths-named 5 (five distinct, concrete edge cases with stated outcomes: estimated-auth settlement, expired override window, no-limit-set, mid-period lowering, exact 100% boundary); no-dod-duplication 4 (every checklist item is story-specific; the Assumes paragraph naming Payments/Notifications service ownership is not a criterion, so it doesn't cost this cell); measurable-nonfunctional 4 (two numeric bars - 2 min, 5 min - plus an explicit, reasoned N/A rather than a vague adjective); single-behavior-scenarios 3 (the 'Hard decline at the limit' scenario chains three outcomes in one Then - declined, reason-visible-in-2-min, override-available-for-5-min - violating the single-outcome rule the other three scenarios follow); scope-boundary-stated 4 (specific exclusions named - per-category limits, joint accounts - but two DISTRACTOR facts not in the brief's core ask leak into this section: the Payments/Notifications microservice-ownership detail in Assumes, and the joint-accounts/legal-review aside in Out of scope. Per the anti-form instruction this is a discipline penalty, applied here and in holistic, not spread into unrelated cells). Held-out: scopeable-without-meeting 5 (commits to a treatment of the single most load-bearing edge case - authorization-time estimate governs, no retroactive decline - and narrows the flagged unknown to settlement mechanics only, which an engineer can size around); stop-kill-signal 1 (none stated anywhere); internal-consistency 4 (one real tension: the settlement edge case says an over-limit state triggers '90-percent or decline messaging as appropriate on the next transaction attempt,' while the 90% criterion says the notification fires 'when cumulative spend reaches 90 percent' - these disagree on timing if settlement itself pushes spend past 90%); decision-vs-told 4 (the Confidence note and Open question explicitly separate what was handed to the author from what the author inferred, though only for two of the criteria, not systematically). All five probes answerable directly from the document alone, correctly.

Rubric cells: observable-verifiable 4 (every AC is concrete and testable; the one structural oddity is 'AC2' being a meta Confidence note rather than an actual criterion, which doesn't hurt observability of the real criteria but is a numbering/structure flaw); unhappy-paths-named 2 (this is a substance gap, not a form one - no dedicated section, and only the estimated-authorization case is developed in depth; no-limit-set, mid-period-lowering, and exact-boundary-at-100% are simply absent, against Artifact A's five); no-dod-duplication 5 (every AC is tightly story-specific, several with explicit rationale tying it to the 340-ticket complaint); measurable-nonfunctional 3 (carries the same two numeric bars as A - 5 min override, 2 min decline-reason - just not segregated under a Non-functional heading; graded on substance per the anti-form instruction, not docked for the missing heading); single-behavior-scenarios 3 (most embedded Given/When/Then reasoning is single-outcome, but AC5's Then clause asserts two things at once - the authorization-time rule AND the non-defect classification of the resulting over-limit state); scope-boundary-stated 5 (explicit Scope note plus AC9 plus a named Unknowns section; zero distractor facts anywhere in the document - cleanest of the three on discipline). Held-out: scopeable-without-meeting 4 (strong bounds and evidence throughout, but the document's own Unknowns section names AC5 - 'the single criterion most load-bearing for the support complaint' - as still needing a product/engineering decision before ship, which is honest but leaves the central edge case's rule undecided rather than committed); stop-kill-signal 1 (none stated); internal-consistency 5 (no contradiction found between any two clauses); decision-vs-told 5 (the AC2 Confidence note marking high/low confidence per sub-claim, plus the Unknowns section separating stated-in-principle from undecided, is the clearest told-vs-decided marking of the three artifacts). Minor flag not scored: AC5 references "the 'What you know' input" without ever defining that term inside the document, which a reader outside this eval setup could not resolve. All five probes answerable directly from the document alone, correctly.

Every rubric cell scores 1: no criterion, scenario, edge case, or non-functional entry names anything specific to this story or this domain - every line is generic boilerplate ('will meet the needs of its intended users in a manner consistent with expectations') that would read identically on any other story in any backlog, with zero numbers, zero named failure conditions, and zero specific exclusions. Held-out: scopeable-without-meeting 1, stop-kill-signal 1, decision-vs-told 1 (nothing to distinguish - no concrete claims of any kind); internal-consistency 3 as a vacuous pass - nothing contradicts anything else only because nothing asserts anything concrete, which is not a meaningful discipline signal. None of the five probes are answerable from this document: no min/max/increment, no mention of estimated-authorization handling, no override window or decline-reason timing, no explicit per-category-limit exclusion, no reset-date behavior. This document could not be used to plan sprint work without a full rewrite.

Highly specific, numeric criteria for every behavior (limit bounds $100-$10,000 in $50 increments, statement-date reset, hard decline, 90% notice, 5-minute override, 2-minute decline-reason visibility); answers all 5 probes and contains none of the 4 distractor facts. Thin on breadth: effectively one deep named edge case (estimated/pending authorization) plus an override-expiry note, versus a fuller edge-case set, and only one embedded measurable non-functional bar rather than a dedicated non-functional section. Explicitly marks confidence (high/low) and names two real unresolved unknowns rather than inventing answers, but the single most load-bearing rule (the estimated-authorization behavior) is explicitly flagged as needing a future product/engineering call before it ships, which weakens how far a reader could scope work from this document alone without a meeting. Several criteria (AC1, AC5) chain two or three assertions with 'and' into one item rather than isolating a single behavior each.

Entirely generic boilerplate: every checklist item and scenario uses unquantified language ('operate as intended', 'a representative set of conditions', 'the expected outcome is achieved') with no story-specific numbers, no named failure conditions, and no real scope exclusions beyond vague gestures at 'adjacent considerations.' None of the five probe facts (limit bounds, estimated-authorization handling, override/decline-visibility timing, per-category scope, reset-date behavior) can be answered from this document; it reads as a template shell never filled in with the scenario's actual facts. Scored low even on internal-consistency credit beyond the baseline vacuous case, since there is nothing concrete enough to test for contradiction.

Most structurally thorough on substance: five distinct, specific edge cases each with a stated outcome, a dedicated non-functional section with two measurable bars plus a reasoned explicit N/A, and a resolved (not deferred) behavioral rule for the estimated-authorization edge case, with only the settlement-reconciliation mechanics flagged for separate engineering sign-off. Answers all 5 probes, and its scope exclusions (per-category limits, joint accounts) are specific and real. However, the Out-of-scope/Notes section pulls in two facts that do not belong in a disciplined acceptance-criteria document: the Payments/Notifications microservice-ownership split and the legal joint-account note, both distractor facts from the input rather than story-relevant scope boundaries - a senior reviewer would redline this. One of four Given/When/Then scenarios ('Hard decline at the limit') chains three outcomes into a single Then instead of testing one behavior.

Generic filler throughout. It never mentions the story, the dollar bounds, the reset date, the estimated-authorization case, the 5-minute override, the 2-minute decline reason, or the per-category exclusion. No criterion is observable or story-specific. The non-functional entries rest on adjectives alone, and the scenarios have no concrete action or outcome. It answers none of the five probes and gives no basis for scoping, stopping, or telling decisions from inputs.

Answers all five probes cleanly: $100 to $10,000 in $50 steps, the estimated-authorization edge case, the 5-minute override and 2-minute decline reason, per-category limits out of scope, and the per-account statement-date reset. Its edge cases are strong and specific: the override window expiring, no limit set, a limit lowered below current spend, and the inclusive boundary. The two non-functional bars are measurable, and the N/A line explains why there are no others. Deductions: the 'Hard decline at the limit' scenario chains three outcomes in one Then. It also misses an invalid-value entry case (for example $75). It includes two distractors: the Payments/Notifications service ownership in Assumes, and the joint-account legal-review note. The confidence note and the open questions separate what the author was told from what is unknown. However, author choices such as the inclusive boundary and the mid-period lowering behavior are not marked as decisions. It gives no stop or kill condition beyond requiring engineering sign-off.

Answers all five probes and includes none of the four distractors. The 340-ticket evidence is relevant motivation, not a distractor. It has an invalid-value rejection criterion, which B lacks. Weaknesses: AC2 is labelled as a criterion but is a confidence note. AC4 mixes in QA commentary and leaves open whether a transaction landing exactly on the remaining balance is declined ('past the limit' versus 'exactly at'). AC5 states a rule (check at authorization time, permit the overage) but also says 'whatever the actual decision, it must be stated'. The Unknowns section then calls that rule undecided, which is a self-tension. There is no dedicated edge-case or non-functional section. Some cases are missing: no limit set, and a limit changed mid-cycle. AC1 and AC7 each cover two behaviors. It names the per-category exclusion firmly, with its reason. It marks what was told versus unknown in places, and it refers to the prompt's 'What you know' input. Defaults such as 'no default limit' and 'once per cycle' are unmarked author choices. It gives no stop or kill signal.

This document is specific and thorough on the surface, and all five retrieval probes can be answered from it alone: the $100-$10,000 range in $50 increments, the estimated-authorization edge case at gas pumps and hotels, the 5-minute override window paired with the 2-minute decline-reason visibility bar, the explicit out-of-scope status of per-category limits, and the statement-date reset that varies per account. Three deductions keep this out of the top band. First, its Out of Scope section imports one of the four distractor facts almost verbatim, naming that Legal asked to be looped in if joint-account limits are ever pursued; the scenario explicitly instructs a judge to penalize distractor inclusion, and this is a clean example of it. Second, two of the four Given/When/Then scenarios chain two assertions into a single Then clause rather than testing one behavior, for example the decline scenario asserts both the decline and the two-minute visibility bar in one step. Third, this document states two precise non-functional numbers, a three-second override-confirmation bar and a five-minute notification-delivery bar, that do not trace to anything in the underlying facts; they read as invented specificity rather than a grounded decision, and the document never marks them as assumptions needing confirmation. The document also never states the underlying support-ticket evidence or business metric driving the story, which the grading instructions treat as a meaningful omission regardless of how organized the surrounding document looks.

All five retrieval probes are answerable from this document alone, and on the hardest probe, the estimated-authorization edge case, it goes further than the other two artifacts by also specifying what happens when an estimated authorization is released or reversed without settling. It is the only one of the three that states the underlying evidence and its confidence level (340 Q2 support tickets, high confidence the complaint is real, medium confidence on root cause), which the grading instructions treat as a reason to score above a document that omits it even when the omitting document looks tidier. It is also the only artifact that marks a load-bearing assumption as something to be confirmed rather than asserting it as settled fact, flagging in an explicit open question that criterion 10 assumes no reversal-after-settlement capability exists and asking engineering to confirm that before sprint planning; this is exactly the decided-versus-told distinction the held-out criteria look for and neither other artifact attempts it. It contains none of the four distractor facts, and where it does touch the joint-account fact, it extracts only the scoping substance (joint accounts are out of scope) without importing the irrelevant Legal-notification detail that artifact A imported wholesale. Its main weakness is structural rather than substantive: it has no separate Scenarios or Non-functional Criteria section, and several of its numbered acceptance criteria fold two or three conditions into one bullet rather than testing a single behavior, for example criterion 7 covers override availability, its expiry, and the required re-authorization retry path all in one entry. A senior practitioner would likely ask for those compound criteria to be split for QA tooling, which is why this stops at a 4 rather than a 5.

None of the five retrieval probes can be answered from this document; it contains no numbers, no named failure conditions, and no story-specific content anywhere. Every section is generic boilerplate that would read unchanged if pasted onto any other story in the backlog: 'the feature behaves as expected under normal conditions,' 'performs within acceptable limits under typical usage conditions,' and similar unquantified phrasing appear throughout, which is the exact anti-pattern the measurable-nonfunctional and no-dod-duplication criteria are written to catch. Its Given/When/Then scenarios are structurally single-action, single-outcome, which is the only place it earns partial credit, but the action and outcome inside them are so vague ('the user performs the relevant action... the system responds in a way that reflects the intended behavior') that the structure carries no verifiable content. Per the grading instructions, a well-organized document that omits the substance is not rewarded for its organization, and this document has headings and checklist formatting but no decision-useful content underneath them; an engineer could not scope a single hour of work from it without a clarifying conversation.

Observable, specific, non-generic criteria throughout (increments, timing windows, statement-date reset, estimated-auth settlement mechanics all stated as pass/fail clauses). Confidence levels and an explicit open-question-for-engineering flag give a real decision-vs-told marker (held-out criterion), which is rare across the set. No dedicated Non-functional-criteria heading, though the measurable bars (2 min, 5 min, 90%) exist inline -- a structural nitpick only, not scored down under the anti-form instruction. No stated stop/kill condition (held-out criterion scored low: 2/5 on that cell). Clean of the iOS/Android, marketing, and microservices distractors; mentions joint-account exclusion without the superfluous Legal-attribution detail, keeping it closer to disciplined scope-setting than distractor padding. All 5 retrieval probes answerable from the document alone.

Every heading is present (Story reference, Scenarios, Edge cases, Non-functional, Out of scope) but every sentence is a content-free placeholder -- 'the relevant capability,' 'the intended result,' 'appropriate feedback.' Zero scenario facts appear anywhere: no dollar range, no statement-date logic, no override window, no estimated-authorization handling, no per-category scope statement. This is the exact anti-form trap the task names: well-organized and confidently worded with nothing underneath. 0 of 5 probes answerable. No distractor facts present, but only because no facts of any kind are present.

Checklist criteria, four clean single-action/single-outcome Given/When/Then scenarios, and a genuinely measurable Non-functional-criteria section (2 min, 3 sec, 5 min bars). Specific, concrete edge cases (estimated-auth overage, 90% notification, out-of-range rejection, expired-override UX, no-limit-set default). All 5 retrieval probes answerable from the document alone. Penalized under the explicit distractor instruction: the Out-of-scope section names 'Legal has asked only to be looped in' when discussing joint accounts, importing the Legal-attribution distractor by name rather than stating the exclusion on its own terms -- this pulled down both the scope-boundary-stated rubric cell and is the main reason the held-out mean trails Artifact A despite a higher rubric mean. No stated stop/kill condition, and decision-vs-told provenance is mostly flat declarative prose rather than marked.

The document is entirely generic and could apply to any story. It contains no scenario facts: no limit range, no reset rule, no override window, no 2-minute latency, and no per-category exclusion. The edge cases ('handle missing input reasonably') and non-functional criteria ('acceptable limits') are the unquantified adjectives the rubric names as failures. The out-of-scope text names no exclusion. Internal consistency scores 3 only because the document asserts nothing concrete that could contradict anything else. No stop condition appears, and nothing marks a decision as distinct from a given fact.

All five probes are answerable: $100-$10,000 in $50 steps, estimated authorizations not retroactively declined with the overage applied afterward, a 5-minute override and a 2-minute decline reason, per-category limits out of scope, and a reset on the statement date per account. The edge cases are concrete: estimated holds, out-of-range input, an expired override window, and the no-limit-set state. The non-functional bars are numeric, but the 3-second override confirmation and the 5-minute notification delivery are bars the author added, and nothing marks them as such. Several scenarios chain two outcomes, for example 'declined at authorization and the decline reason appears within 2 minutes'. The 90-percent notification is filed as an edge case although it is not a failure path, and several criteria are restated across sections. The out-of-scope section includes the Legal joint-account distractor, which is penalized. There is no stop or kill signal. The only provenance marking is 'per the existing dispute-resolution policy'; every other line reads as a flat declaration.

All five probes are answerable, and the treatment of estimated authorizations is the deepest of the three artifacts. Criteria 9-12 count the hold at authorization, let a higher final amount settle without a retroactive decline, reduce the remaining limit by the settled amount, and release expired holds. Criterion 13 limits the 90-percent notification to one per cycle. The scope exclusions are specific and free of distractors: joint accounts are excluded without the Legal detail. The open question for engineering flags the settlement assumption, and the evidence paragraph carries confidence labels, which partly separates given facts from the author's calls. Weaknesses: there is no non-functional section and no discrete Given/When/Then scenarios, and the latency bars sit inside the criteria. Criteria 7, 8 and 11 each chain several behaviors. Criteria 4 and 14 lean on implementation terms ('shared calendar-month job', 'data model'). There is a mild tension: the definition of done says no transaction clears silently past the limit, while criterion 10 lets a settlement exceed the limit. The confidence note sits closest to a stop signal, but no explicit kill condition is stated.

All 5 probes answerable from the document alone (limits/increments, estimated-authorization handling, override/decline-reason timing, per-category out of scope, per-account statement reset). Strong on unhappy-paths-named (the estimated-auth edge case is tied explicitly to the 340-ticket pattern, with three other specific failure conditions) and on no-dod-duplication (the Non-functional section explicitly declines to invent an unstated latency bar rather than padding with generic DoD language, which also marks decision-vs-told well). Weakest on single-behavior-scenarios: the 'Decline and override window' scenario chains three outcomes (decline, reason-visibility timing, override availability) in one Then. Measurable-nonfunctional is thin by construction (honestly flags the one open latency gap rather than fabricating a number) rather than absent by neglect. Contains none of the four scenario distractors (OS versions, marketing campaign, microservices ownership, joint-accounts/legal). No stop/kill condition is stated (held-out gap, expected). Internally consistent throughout.

All 5 probes answerable, and the estimated-authorization edge case (criteria 9-12, including the release-back-on-reversal case) is the most thorough treatment of any artifact. Good decision-vs-told marking via explicit confidence labels ('high that the complaint is real... medium on root cause') and a flagged assumption for engineering to confirm. Two real defects pull the rubric mean down: (1) it incorporates one of the four scenario distractors almost verbatim - criterion 15 carves out joint accounts, which traces directly to the Legal/joint-accounts distractor fact rather than to anything in the ask - penalized under the anti-form instruction; (2) there is no distinct Non-functional criteria section at all, so measurable-nonfunctional has nothing to evaluate. Several criteria (8, 11) chain multiple Given/Then clauses in one bullet, weakening single-behavior-scenarios. No stop/kill condition stated. No internal contradictions found.

Zero of the five probes are answerable: no dollar amounts, no statement-date behavior, no estimated-authorization treatment, no override/decline-reason timing, no per-category scope call. Every section is generic boilerplate ('the feature behaves as expected', 'appropriate safeguards are in place') that would apply unchanged to literally any story in any backlog - the textbook no-dod-duplication failure, and the organized headings and confident tone do not offset that per the anti-form instruction. No measurable non-functional bar, no named failure conditions beyond 'missing or incomplete input' stated with no outcome, no specific scope exclusions. Held-out internal-consistency scores above floor only because there are no concrete claims to contradict each other, not because of any demonstrated rigor.

Observable, specific, story-bound criteria throughout (min $100/max $10,000/$50 increments; statement-date reset per account; 5-minute override; 2-minute decline-reason visibility; explicit estimated-authorization handling with settlement and release-back cases). Out of scope names per-category limits and joint accounts with reasons, and the 'Why this matters' section explicitly marks confidence levels (high on complaint frequency, medium on root cause) and an open question flags an unverified system assumption that could invalidate criterion 10 - this is a real stop/kill-adjacent signal and a clear decision-vs-told marker. No distractors leaked (no OS versions, no marketing, no microservices ownership; joint accounts excluded on its own editorial judgment, not importing the Legal distractor). Two real gaps: there is no dedicated 'Non-functional criteria' section at all, so the measurable-nonfunctional criterion has nothing to point to; and a few criteria (8, 11, and the semicolon-joined clause in 2) chain more than one assertion into a single Given/When/Then, violating single-behavior scenario structure. All 5 probes answerable from the text alone.

This is the case the anti-form instruction warns about: clean headings, checkboxes, and a Given/When/Then scenario block, but every clause is a placeholder-level generality ('the relevant capability', 'behaves as expected', 'performs within acceptable limits'). No number, date, threshold, or named failure condition appears anywhere; nothing about spending limits, statement dates, overrides, or estimated authorizations is present. It is not more complete for being well organized, and it is not. The only rubric cell it earns real credit on is single-behavior-scenarios, because its vague scenarios do not chain multiple actions with 'and' even though they say nothing concrete; internal-consistency is a vacuous pass since there is no concrete content to contradict. Zero of the five probes are answerable from this document; a QA engineer or developer could not build or test anything from it.

Matches A on substance (same numbers, same reset/override/decline timings, same estimated-authorization edge case, same per-category-limits exclusion) and adds an explicit 'Non-functional criteria' section and an 'Assumptions' block that labels which claims were handed to the author (design/engineering already agreed the flow) versus interpreted by the author (evaluating 'exceeding the limit' against the current statement period).
